## Part A — Creating Data Frames

```{r}
name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```

```{r}
students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
students
```

```{r}
typeof(students$name)
class(students$name)
```

```{r}

  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 2),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)

courses
```

Question 2.

Lists in R are heterogeneous data structures, meaning different elements in a list can store different data types. Atomic vectors in R are homogeneous, meaning all elements inside a single vector must be of the exact same data type.

## Part D — Data Frame Operations

```{r}
students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
students
```

```{r}
students$passed <- NULL
students
```

```{r}
students[order(students$age), ]
```

```{r}
students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```
Question 7.

No, you cannot successfully filter by passed after removing it. Attempting students$passed == TRUE will return logical(0) because students$passed evaluates to NULL.

Question 8.

students$age extracts the numeric vector of ages: c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20). order(students$age) computes the row positions required to sort the vector from smallest to largest, returning the index vector c(3, 1, 5, 2, 4). Passing this vector into the row slot of matrix notation students[c(3, 1, 5, 2, 4), ] instructs R to retrieve row 3 first, followed by row 1, row 5, row 2, and row 4. Leaving the column slot blank after the comma , signals to R that all columns (name, age, year_level) should be kept for each reordered row, maintaining the integrity of each student's record.   

## Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average < 80, "Failed", "Passed")
grades
```
Question 9.

First, create a different column calculate a new column called grade_change <- grades$final - grades$midterm to quantify score increases or drops for each student. Secondly, filter students use logical subsetting (grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", ]) to extract all students who received a "Failed" remark into a separate view. Lastly,Use order() to sort the failed students by midterm score in ascending order, and then sort by grade_change. By comparing whether failing students primarily had low initial midterm scores or large negative grade drops, the instructor can determine which factor correlates more strongly with failing.


## Conclusion 

A data frame is a two-dimensional, grid-like data structure where rows correspond to individual observations and columns represent variables. Under the hood, a data frame is built as a named list of equal-length vectors, allowing each column to hold its own distinct data type (such as numeric, character, or logical). This flexibility makes data frames R's primary structure for real-world tabular datasets, as real data naturally combines quantitative metrics and qualitative descriptors within the same table.
